Lab 10: Point Intervals and Estimates

Jason M. Klemm

2026-07-26

Given Information

The set of log likelihood functions:

logbin <- function(x,param) log(dbinom(x,prob = param,size = 20))
logpoiss <- function(x,param) log(dpois(x,lambda = param)) 
logexp <- function(x,param) log(dexp(x,rate = param))

The general function used to find the maximum likelihood estimate of a one parameter likelihood using grid approximation:

mymaxlik <- function(lfun,x,param,...){
  # how manyparam values are there?
  np <- length(param)
  # outer -- notice the order, x then param
  # this produces a matrix -- try outer(1:4,5:10,function(x,y) paste(x,y,sep=" "))   to understand
  z <- outer(x,param,lfun)
  # z is a matrix where each x,param is replaced with the function evaluated at those values
  
  y <- apply(z,2,sum)
  
  # y is a vector made up of the column sums
  # Each y is the log lik for a new parameter value
  
  plot(param,
       y,
       col="Blue",
       type="l",
       lwd=2,
       ...)
  
  # which gives the index for the value of y == max.
  # there could be a max between two values of the parameter, therefore 2 indices
  # the first max will take the larger index
  i <- max(which.max(y))
  
  abline(v=param[i],
         lwd=2,
         col="Red")
  
  # plots a nice point where the max lik is
  points(param[i],
         y[i],
         pch=19,
         cex=1.5,
         col="Black")
  
  axis(3,
       param[i],
       round(param[i],2))
  
  #check slopes. If it is a max the slope shoud change sign from + to -
  # We should get three + and two -
  ifelse(i-3 >= 1 & i+2 <= np, 
         slope <-  (y[(i-2):(i+2)]-y[(i-3):(i+1)])/(param[(i-2):(i+2)]-param[(i-3):(i+1)]),
         slope <- "NA")
  
  return(invisible(list(i = i,
                        parami = param[i],
                        yi = y[i],
                        slope = slope)
  ))
}

Task 1

Using mymaxlik() find the maximum likelihood estimate for \(𝑝\) the probability of success when \(3\) independent binomial experiments are repeated with \(𝑛=20\) the result was x=c(9,10,11) successes.

  • Using \(LATEX\) write the likelihood for this experiment.

  • Give the returned named list from the function call. Please explain each part.

  • Interpret the plot produced.

Part a

Since we know that \(Y_i\sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) where we have \(3\) independent experiments with \(n=20\) and \(Y_1 = 9\), \(Y_2 = 10\), \(Y_3 = 11\) we can the write the likelihood as follows:

\[L(p) = p(y_1)\cdot p(y_2)\cdot p(y_3) = \binom{20}{9}p^9q^{11} \cdot \binom{20}{10}p^{10}q^{10} \cdot \binom{20}{11}p^{11}q^{9} = \binom{20}{9}\binom{20}{10}\binom{20}{11}p^{30}q^{30} = \binom{20}{9}\binom{20}{10}\binom{20}{11}p^{30}(1-p)^{30}\]

Therefore the likelihood for this experiment is:

\[L(p) = \binom{20}{9}\binom{20}{10}\binom{20}{11}p^{30}(1-p)^{30}\]

Part b

Below is the function call:

# Run function - update logbin to have size = 20
results1 <- mymaxlik(lfun = logbin, x = c(9,10,11), param = seq(0, 1, by = 0.001), ylab = expression(log(L(p))), xlab = expression(p))

# Result output
results1
## $i
## [1] 501
## 
## $parami
## [1] 0.5
## 
## $yi
## [1] -5.399077
## 
## $slope
## [1]  0.6000156  0.3600036  0.1200002 -0.1200002 -0.3600036

Interpretation of results

i:

This represents the index of the maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat{p}\). In other words this is the index of probability \(p\) from our grid where the log-likelihood function reaches its peak. From our result we can see that this index value is \(501\) on our grid.

parami:

This is the value at our index i and is the maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat{p}\). In other words this is the probability \(p\) from our grid where the log-likelihood function reaches its peak. From our result we can see that \(\hat{p}=0.5\), meaning the probability of success for each trial in the binomial experiment is estimated to be \(50\%\).

yi:

This is the maximum log likelihood value that corresponds to \(\hat{p}\) from parami. From our result we can see that the log likelihood value at \(\hat{p}\) is \(-5.3991\).

slope:

This result collects slopes around the indexed \(\hat{p}\) and shows that the slope of the log-likelihood function changes signs to confirm that the indexed value is the maximum. We should be getting three positive slopes and then two negative slopes. This is essentially using the first derivative test to show that parami is indeed the maximum because the slopes taken from both sides of it change sign. From our result we can see that this holds true as the slope goes from approximately \(0.60\) to \(0.36\) to \(0.12\) to \(-0.12\) then \(-0.36\).

Part c

Interpretation of the plot

The plot produced shows a symmetric curve of the log likelihood function where the maximum log likelihood occurs directly at \(p=0.5\) as indicated by the point in black and red vertical line. The fact that this plot is symmetric around this maximum makes sense given that the exponents on both \(p\) and \((1-p)\) were \(30\). This meaning that both the probability of success and failure weigh equally in the likelihood function and that they were equal right at \(p=0.5\).

Task 2

Suppose a radioactive source is disintegrating with rate \(\lambda\) particles/sec. A sample of \(4\) measurements were made on the rate, they were y=c(5,5,6,7) particles/sec.

Use mymaxlik() function to find the grid estimate for \(\lambda\).

  • What is the distribution of \(Y_i\)?

  • Use mymaxlik() and show the plot and returned list.

  • Interpret the returned list.

Part a

Given that the problem uses \(\lambda\) and involves the disintegration rate of particles from a radioactive source, where the rate represents the relative frequency of an event over a period of time, \(Y_i\sim \mathrm{}Pois(\lambda)\).

Part b

Below is the function call:

# Run function 
results2 <- mymaxlik(lfun = logpoiss, x = c(5,5,6,7), param = seq(0, 20, by = 0.001), ylab = expression(log(L(lambda))), xlab = expression(lambda))

# Result output
results2
## $i
## [1] 5751
## 
## $parami
## [1] 5.75
## 
## $yi
## [1] -7.447799
## 
## $slope
## [1]  0.0017398970  0.0010437606  0.0003478664 -0.0003477858 -0.0010431960

Part c

Interpretation of results

i:

This represents the index of the maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat{\lambda}\). In other words this is the index of disintegration rate \(\lambda\) from our grid where the log-likelihood function reaches its peak. From our result we can see that this index value is \(5751\) on our grid.

parami:

This is the value at our index i and is the maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat{\lambda}\). In other words this is the disintegration rate \(\lambda\) from our grid where the log-likelihood function reaches its peak. From our result we can see that \(\hat{\lambda}=5.75\), meaning the average disintegration rate of the radioactive source is estimated to be \(5.75\) particles/sec.

yi:

This is the maximum log likelihood value that corresponds to \(\hat{\lambda}\) from parami. From our result we can see that the log likelihood value at \(\hat{\lambda}\) is \(-7.4478\).

slope:

This result collects slopes around the indexed \(\hat{\lambda}\) and shows that the slope of the log-likelihood function changes signs to confirm that the indexed value is the maximum. We should be getting three positive slopes and then two negative slopes. This is essentially using the first derivative test to show that parami is indeed the maximum because the slopes taken from both sides of it change sign. From our result we can see that this holds true as the slope goes from approximately \(0.002\) to \(0.001\) to \(0.0003\) to \(-0.0003\) then \(-0.001\).

Task 3

Improve on the estimate of Task 2 by using the following function mymld():

Below is the given function:

logbin = function(x,param) log(dbinom(x,prob=param,size=10))
logpoiss = function(x,param) log(dpois(x,lambda=param)) 


mymld=function(lfun,x,param,delta=0.0001){    # param = parameter values, delta=accuracy, x=data
  z=outer(x,param,lfun)    # create outer product and evaluate at lfun
  y=apply(z,2,sum) # x by param, 2=columns , sum columns = sum of log lik
  
  i=max(which(y==max(y)))# the index for which y is biggest, if two then take the last one
  
  param2=seq(param[i-2],param[i+2],by=delta)# The maximum will be between these two, increments by delta
  zz=outer(x,param2,lfun) # new z, call it zz
  yy=apply(zz,2,sum)   # new y, call it yy
  ii=max(which(yy==max(yy)))# new i,  call it ii , if two, take max of them (last one)
  layout(matrix(c(1,2),nrow = 1,ncol = 2,byrow = TRUE))# divide plotting space for two graphs
  plot(param,y,col = "Blue",type = "l",lwd = 2,ylab = "Log. Lik.",xlab = expression(theta))# plot log lik Vs parameter values
  abline(v=param[i],lwd=2,col="Red") # Show vertical line at estimated value          
  axis(3,param[i],round(param[i],2))
  points(param[i],y[i],pch=19,cex=1.5,col="Black")# Plot the point
  plot(param2,yy,col="Blue",type="l",lwd=2,ylab="Log. Lik.",xlab=expression(theta)) # construct new plot for refined estimate
  abline(v=param2[ii],lwd=2,col="Red")  # new verical line
  val=round(param2[ii],abs(log10(delta))) ## rounds to the nth place where n is st delta=10^-n.         
  axis(3,param2[ii],val)
  points(param2[ii],yy[ii],pch=19,cex=1.5,col="Black")
  v <- param2[ii]
  v
}

Below is the function call using the same problem as in Task 2:

# Run function 
results3 <- mymld(lfun = logpoiss, x = c(5,5,6,7), param = seq(0, 20, by = 0.001))

# Result output
results3
## [1] 5.75

After running the new function mymld() we get the same result where \(\hat{\lambda}=5.75\). Both methods agree because the sample mean is \(5.75\) (\(\bar{y} = \frac{5+5+6+7}{4}\)). However using this new method as seen from the right plot allows for a more fine detailed approach to visualizing and calculating the maximum likelihood estimate. Instead of taking a birds-eye view around the maximum we zoom in to where it is likely to be and find the estimate to a greater level of accuracy.

Task 4

We are given the following function:

mymaxlikg=function(lfun, theta) { # default log lik is a combination bin
  nth <- length(theta)  # nu. of values used in theta
  thmat <- matrix(theta,nr=nth,nc=1,byrow=TRUE) # Matrix of theta
  z <- apply(thmat,1,lfun) # z holds the log lik values
  zmax <- max(which(z==max(z)))  # finding the INDEX of the max lik
  plot(theta,exp(z),type="l") # plot of lik
  abline(v=theta[zmax],col="Blue")   #  verical line through max
  axis(3,theta[zmax],round(theta[zmax],4))  # one tick on the third axis 
  theta[zmax]   # theta corresponding to max lik
}

Use the above function mymaxlikg() with three independent binomial experiments where we assume the same probability of success.

\[X_1 \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n=10,p)\]

\[X_2 \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n=20,p)\]

\[X_3 \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n=30,p)\]

  • Change the function code so that the plot will be correctly labelled.

  • In this case \(X_1=4\), \(X_2=12\) and \(X_3=7\) – find the maximum likelihood estimate using mymaxlikg()

Part a

Changing the code we can get the plot correctly labelled as follows:

# Correct function plot labels
mymaxlikg_new=function(lfun, theta) { # default log lik is a combination bin
  nth <- length(theta)  # nu. of values used in theta
  thmat <- matrix(theta,nr=nth,nc=1,byrow=TRUE) # Matrix of theta
  z <- apply(thmat,1,lfun) # z holds the log lik values
  zmax <- max(which(z==max(z)))  # finding the INDEX of the max lik
  plot(theta,exp(z),type="l", ylab = expression(L(p)), xlab = expression(p)) # plot of lik
  abline(v=theta[zmax],col="Blue", lwd = 2)   #  verical line through max
  axis(3,theta[zmax],round(theta[zmax],4))  # one tick on the third axis 
  theta[zmax]   # theta corresponding to max lik
}

Part b

Below is the function call:

# Can do this because the product of logs is a sum
logbin_task4=function(theta){log(dbinom(4,prob=theta,size=10)) + log(dbinom(12,prob=theta,size=20)) + log(dbinom(7,prob=theta,size=30))}

# Run corrected function
results4 <- mymaxlikg_new(lfun = logbin_task4, theta = seq(0, 1, by = 0.0001))

results4
## [1] 0.3833

The results indicate that the maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat{p} \approx 0.3833\). This meaning that the probability of success for each trial in the binomial experiment is estimated to be \(\sim 38\%\).

Task 5

We are given the following function:

mymlnorm=function(x,mu,sig,...){  #x sample vector
  nmu=length(mu) # number of values in mu
  nsig=length(sig)
  n=length(x) # sample size
  zz=c()    ## initialize a new vector
  lfun=function(x,m,p) log(dnorm(x,mean=m,sd=p))   # log lik for normal
  for(j in 1:nsig){
    z=outer(x,mu,lfun,p=sig[j]) # z a matrix 
    # col 1 of z contains lfun evaluated at each x with first value of mu, 
    # col2 each x with 2nd value of m 
    # all with sig=sig[j]
    y=apply(z,2,sum)
    # y is a vector filled with log lik values, 
    # each with a difft mu and all with the same sig[j]
    zz=cbind(zz,y)
    ## zz is the matrix with each column containing log L values, rows difft mu, cols difft sigmas 
  }
  maxl=max(exp(zz))
  coord=which(exp(zz)==maxl,arr.ind=TRUE)
  maxlsig=apply(zz,1,max)
  contour(mu,sig,exp(zz),las=3,xlab=expression(mu),ylab=expression(sigma),axes=TRUE,
          main=expression(paste("L(",mu,",",sigma,")",sep="")),...)
  mlx=round(mean(x),2)  # theoretical
  mly=round(sqrt((n-1)/n)*sd(x),2)
  #axis(1,at=c(0:20,mlx),labels=sort(c(0:20,mlx)))
  #axis(2,at=c(0:20,mly),labels=TRUE)
  abline(v=mean(x),lwd=2,col="Green")
  abline(h=sqrt((n-1)/n)*sd(x),lwd=2,col="Red")
  
  # Now find the estimates from the co-ords
  muest=mu[coord[1]]
  sigest=sig[coord[2]]
  
  abline(v=muest, h=sigest)
  return(list(x=x,muest = muest, sigest = sigest,maxl=maxl))
}

  • Suppose x=c(5,7,7,8,10) is a sample from a Normal distribution – use mymlnorm() to find maximum likelihood estimates for \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).

  • Show the plots and the returned list output – interpret the output.

Part a

Below is the function call:

# Run function 
results5 <- mymlnorm(x = c(5,7,7,8,10), mu = seq(5, 10, by = 0.01), sig = seq(0.5, 4, by = 0.01))

# Result output
results5
## $x
## [1]  5  7  7  8 10
## 
## $muest
## [1] 7.4
## 
## $sigest
## [1] 1.62
## 
## $maxl
## [1] 7.324622e-05

Part b

Interpretation of results

x:

This is the vector of x values that represents our sample.

muest:

This is the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\hat{\mu}\) for the data we supplied. The result here gives \(\hat{\mu} = 7.4\) and this means that the estimated average of the population is \(7.4\).

sigest:

This is the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\hat{\sigma}\) for the data we supplied. The result here gives \(\hat{\sigma} = 1.62\) and this means that the estimated standard deviation of the population is \(1.62\).

maxl:

This is the value of the likelihood function when evaluated at our estimates of \(\hat{\mu}=7.4\) and \(\hat{\sigma}=1.62\). It represents the maximum height (joint probability density) achieved by the likelihood surface.

Task 6

We are given the following function:

mynewt=function(x0,delta=0.001,f,fdash, xlim = c(-x0,x0)){
  d <- 100
  i <- 0
  x <- c()
  y <- c()
  x[1] <- x0
  y[1] <- f(x[1])
  while(d > delta & i < 1000){
    i <- i+1
    x[i+1] <- x[i] - f(x[i])/fdash(x[i])
    y[i+1] <- f(x[i+1])
    d <- abs(y[i])
  }
  #windows()
  curve(f(x),
        xlim = xlim,
        xaxt = "n", 
        main = "Newton-Raphson Algorithm")
  
  points(x,
         y,
         col = "Red",
         pch = 19,
         cex = 1.5)
  
  axis(1,x,round(x,2),las=2)
  abline(h = 0,col = "Red")
  
  segments(x[1:(i-1)],y[1:(i-1)],x[2:i],rep(0,i-1),col="Blue",lwd=2)
  segments(x[2:i],rep(0,i-1),x[2:i],y[2:i],lwd=0.5,col="Pink")
  
  list(x = x,y = y)
}

Part b

I will use both different approximation updates being:

\[f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\]

\[f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h/2)-f(x-h/2)}{h}\]

Doing so with the first:

mynewt_1=function(x0,delta=0.001,f, xlim = c(-x0,x0)){
  d <- 100
  i <- 0
  x <- c()
  y <- c()
  x[1] <- x0
  y[1] <- f(x[1])
  h <- 0.000001 # get as close to 0 as possible
  fdash <- function(x, h){
    
    (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
    
  }
  while(d > delta & i < 1000){
    i <- i+1
    x[i+1] <- x[i] - f(x[i])/fdash(x[i],h)
    y[i+1] <- f(x[i+1])
    d <- abs(y[i])
  }
  #windows()
  curve(f(x),
        xlim = xlim,
        xaxt = "n", 
        main = "Newton-Raphson Algorithm")
  
  points(x,
         y,
         col = "Red",
         pch = 19,
         cex = 1.5)
  
  axis(1,x,round(x,2),las=2)
  abline(h = 0,col = "Red")
  
  segments(x[1:(i-1)],y[1:(i-1)],x[2:i],rep(0,i-1),col="Blue",lwd=2)
  segments(x[2:i],rep(0,i-1),x[2:i],y[2:i],lwd=0.5,col="Pink")
  
  list(x = x,y = y)
}

mynewt_2=function(x0,delta=0.001,f, xlim = c(-x0,x0)){
  d <- 100
  i <- 0
  x <- c()
  y <- c()
  x[1] <- x0
  y[1] <- f(x[1])
  h <- 0.000001 # get as close to 0 as possible
  fdash <- function(x, h){
    
    (f(x + h/2) - f(x - h/2)) / h
    
  }
  while(d > delta & i < 1000){
    i <- i+1
    x[i+1] <- x[i] - f(x[i])/fdash(x[i],h)
    y[i+1] <- f(x[i+1])
    d <- abs(y[i])
  }
  #windows()
  curve(f(x),
        xlim = xlim,
        xaxt = "n", 
        main = "Newton-Raphson Algorithm")
  
  points(x,
         y,
         col = "Red",
         pch = 19,
         cex = 1.5)
  
  axis(1,x,round(x,2),las=2)
  abline(h = 0,col = "Red")
  
  segments(x[1:(i-1)],y[1:(i-1)],x[2:i],rep(0,i-1),col="Blue",lwd=2)
  segments(x[2:i],rep(0,i-1),x[2:i],y[2:i],lwd=0.5,col="Pink")
  
  list(x = x,y = y)
}

The application of NR to MLE

We are given the function:

myNRML <- function(x0,delta = 0.001,llik,xrange,parameter = "param"){
  f <- function(x) (llik(x+delta)-llik(x))/delta
  fdash <- function(x) (f(x+delta)-f(x))/delta
  d=1000
  i=0
  x=c()
  y=c()
  x[1]=x0
  y[1]=f(x[1])
  while(d > delta & i<100){
    i=i+1
    x[i+1]=x[i]-f(x[i])/fdash(x[i])
    y[i+1]=f(x[i+1])
    d=abs(y[i+1])
  }
  layout(matrix(1:2,nr=1,nc=2,byrow=TRUE),width=c(1,2))
  curve(llik(x), xlim=xrange,xlab=parameter,ylab="log Lik",main="Log Lik")
  curve(f(x),xlim=xrange,xaxt="n", xlab=parameter,ylab="derivative",main=  "Newton-Raphson Algorithm \n on the derivative")
  points(x,y,col="Red",pch=19,cex=1.5)
  axis(1,x,round(x,2),las=2)
  abline(h=0,col="Red")
  
  segments(x[1:(i-1)],y[1:(i-1)],x[2:i],rep(0,i-1),col="Blue",lwd=2)
  segments(x[2:i],rep(0,i-1),x[2:i],y[2:i],lwd=0.5,col="Green")
  
  list(x=x,y=y)
}

Using the same function myNRML(), create the ML estimate for \(\lambda\) when two Poisson experiments are made with the same disintegrating nuclear substance. The data collected are 3 and 4 particles in one second.

To do this we can do the following function call:

# Run function
myNRML(
  x0 = 0.1, 
  delta = 0.000001, 
  llik = function(x) log(dpois(3, lambda = x) * dpois(4, lambda = x)), 
  xrange = c(0.1, 10), 
  parameter = expression(lambda)
)

Task 7

We are given the following function:

myboot <- function(iter = 10000,x,fun = "mean",alpha = 0.05,cx = 1.5,...){  #Notice where the ... is repeated in the code
  n <- length(x)   #sample size
  
  y <- sample(x, n * iter,replace = TRUE)
  rs.mat <- matrix(y,nr = n,nc = iter,byrow = TRUE)
  xstat <- apply(rs.mat,2,fun) # xstat is a vector and will have iter values in it 
  ci <- quantile(xstat,c(alpha/2,1-alpha/2))# Nice way to form a confidence interval
  # A histogram follows
  # The object para will contain the parameters used to make the histogram
  para <- hist(xstat,
               freq = FALSE,
               las = 1,
               main = paste("Histogram of Bootstrap sample statistics",
                            "\n","alpha=",alpha," iter=",iter,sep=""),
               ...)
  
  #mat will be a matrix that contains the data, this is done so that I can use apply()
  mat <- matrix(x,nr=length(x),nc=1,byrow=TRUE)
  
  #pte is the point estimate
  #This uses whatever fun is
  pte <- apply(mat,2,fun)
  abline(v=pte,lwd=3,col="Black")# Vertical line
  segments(ci[1],0,ci[2],0,lwd=4)      #Make the segment for the ci
  text(ci[1],0,paste("(",round(ci[1],2),sep=""),col="Red",cex=cx)
  text(ci[2],0,paste(round(ci[2],2),")",sep=""),col="Red",cex=cx)
  
  # plot the point estimate 1/2 way up the density
  text(pte,max(para$density)/2,round(pte,2),cex=cx)
  
  invisible(list(ci = ci,fun = fun,x = x))# Some output to use if necessary
}

  • Use myboot() to create a \(95\%\) interval estimate of the mean LMBASS fish WEIGHTS using the DDT data set. Use iter = 10000.

  • Using the same same data set create an interval estimate using t.test().

myboot(iter = 10000, x = ddt$WEIGHT[ddt$SPECIES == "LMBASS"], fun = "mean", alpha = 0.05)

Task 8

The app was modified to be more efficient and is included in the submission. The first change made was to separate re-sampling from the statistic calculations so that simulations only needed to be performed once. In other words, once the number of iterations is defined re-sampling takes place and the resulting matrix then has functions applied to it without having to be be remade. The last two changes made were to update the UI and add a line and text overlay for the point estimate. Below is a screenshot of the working app and the link to access it:
